headings.title: Introduction to Skilled Nursing Facilities
headings.content: Skilled Nursing Facilities (SNFs) play a critical role in the continuum of healthcare, bridging the gap between acute hospital care and independent living or home-based care. For nursing students in Nigeria and globally, understanding SNFs is essential because they cater to frail elderly individuals, chronically ill patients, and those recovering from major surgeries, strokes, or trauma who no longer require acute hospital admission but still need round-the-clock professional medical and nursing attention. Unlike traditional residential care homes that primarily offer custodial or daily living assistance, SNFs are heavily clinical environments. They are specifically designed to deliver subacute care, complex wound management, intravenous therapy, and intensive physical, occupational, or speech rehabilitation. The overarching goal of an SNF is to restore patients to their highest possible level of physical, mental, and psychosocial functioning, promoting independence where feasible, or providing dignified palliative and end-of-life care. Nurses in SNFs must possess strong clinical judgement, patience, and leadership skills to manage complex, multi-system health conditions in an environment that functions both as a long-term home and a short-term rehabilitation center. Recognizing the unique operational and philosophical framework of SNFs allows nursing professionals to deliver holistic, patient-centered care that addresses not only the physiological deficits of the residents but also their emotional and social well-being.

headings.title: Services and Levels of Care Provided
headings.content: Skilled Nursing Facilities provide a comprehensive spectrum of health services tailored to meet the dynamic needs of their resident population. These services are broadly categorized into short-term rehabilitation and long-term chronic care. Short-term care typically involves post-acute rehabilitation for patients recovering from orthopedic surgeries like hip replacements, cardiovascular incidents, or severe infections. These patients usually stay for a few weeks until they regain sufficient strength to return home. Conversely, long-term care residents often live with progressive neurodegenerative disorders, severe cognitive impairments, or advanced frailty requiring permanent institutional support. Clinical services offered within SNFs include complex wound care involving negative pressure wound therapy, intravenous antibiotic administration, total parenteral nutrition (TPN), tracheostomy care, and pain management. In addition to medical and nursing interventions, SNFs provide robust rehabilitative therapies. Physical therapy focuses on mobility, balance, and strength; occupational therapy assists patients in relearning activities of daily living such as dressing, bathing, and eating; and speech-language pathology addresses swallowing disorders (dysphagia) and communication deficits. Dietary and nutritional services are equally vital, ensuring that residents receive customized meal plans to manage chronic conditions like diabetes, hypertension, and renal failure. By integrating these diverse clinical and therapeutic modalities, SNFs ensure that every resident receives comprehensive care targeted to their specific diagnosis and recovery trajectory.

headings.title: Admission Criteria and Patient Eligibility
headings.content: Admission to a Skilled Nursing Facility is governed by specific clinical, functional, and financial criteria to ensure that patients truly require the high level of care provided. Generally, a prospective resident must have a documented physician's order indicating the medical necessity for skilled nursing or rehabilitative services. Many admissions follow a qualifying three-day inpatient hospital stay, particularly for patients utilizing specific insurance or health financing models that require prior acute stabilization. During the pre-admission phase, a thorough clinical evaluation is conducted by the SNF admissions team—often including a registered nurse or social worker—to review the patient's medical history, current medication regimen, functional deficits, and nursing requirements. This assessment ensures the facility has the adequate resources, equipment, and clinical competency to safely care for the individual. For instance, a patient requiring mechanical ventilator support or specialized dialysis cannot be admitted to an SNF unless the facility possesses the specific specialized unit and trained staff to handle such high-acuity needs. Furthermore, psychosocial evaluations are performed to understand the resident's support systems, cognitive status, and behavioral health history. Once eligibility is confirmed, an informed consent process takes place, involving the patient or their legal healthcare proxy, outlining facility policies, expected care plans, and financial responsibilities, thereby establishing a transparent foundation for the resident's stay.

headings.title: The Role of the Nursing Team in SNFs
headings.content: The nursing team forms the operational backbone of any Skilled Nursing Facility, carrying out round-the-clock clinical care, monitoring, and resident advocacy. Staffing typically consists of a mix of Registered Nurses (RNs), Licensed Practical Nurses (LPNs) or Licensed Vocational Nurses (LVNs), and Certified Nursing Assistants (CNAs). RNs usually hold supervisory, assessment, and care-planning roles, managing complex clinical procedures such as intravenous therapy, sterile dressing changes, and emergency response coordination. LPNs/LVNs work under the supervision of RNs, administering oral and injectable medications, monitoring vital signs, documenting clinical observations, and assisting with routine treatments. CNAs provide the vital hands-on, direct-care support that defines daily living in the facility: assisting residents with personal hygiene, feeding, mobility, transferring, and repositioning to prevent pressure injuries. Because nurses spend the most time with residents, they are often the first to detect subtle clinical deteriorations, such as early signs of sepsis, urinary tract infections, dehydration, or changes in cognitive baseline. Beyond direct clinical tasks, the nursing team acts as the primary communication bridge between residents, families, physicians, and other therapists. They ensure that prescribed therapies are integrated into daily routines and that emotional support and compassionate care are consistently delivered, fostering a safe and therapeutic environment for every individual.

headings.title: Interdisciplinary Healthcare Collaboration
headings.content: Optimal care in a Skilled Nursing Facility cannot be achieved by nursing staff alone; it requires cohesive, interdisciplinary healthcare collaboration. The interdisciplinary team (IDT) typically includes physicians, nurse practitioners, RNs, physical therapists, occupational therapists, speech-language pathologists, social workers, registered dietitians, and activity directors. Each discipline brings a specialized lens to the resident's overall health profile. For example, while physical therapists evaluate gait and transfer safety, the registered dietitian assesses nutritional intake and serum albumin levels, and the social worker evaluates emotional adjustment and discharge readiness. Regular IDT meetings are held to review resident progress, evaluate care goals, discuss clinical setbacks, and adjust the care plan accordingly. Effective communication among team members prevents conflicting interventions and ensures that all aspects of the resident's physical, psychological, and social needs are addressed holistically. Nurses play a pivotal coordinating role within the IDT, often acting as the central hub of information. They communicate observations from the bedside to the therapists and physicians, while translating medical orders into practical, round-the-clock nursing interventions. This collaborative approach minimizes medical errors, enhances functional recovery outcomes, reduces unnecessary hospital readmissions, and ensures a high quality of life for all residents residing within the facility.

headings.title: Patient Assessment, Care Planning, and Documentation
headings.content: Structured patient assessment, individualized care planning, and meticulous documentation are foundational pillars of professional nursing practice in Skilled Nursing Facilities. Upon admission, nurses and the interdisciplinary team conduct comprehensive baseline assessments covering clinical history, skin integrity, fall risk, cognitive function, pain levels, and nutritional status. Standardized assessment tools, such as the Minimum Data Set (MDS) in many regulatory frameworks, are utilized to systematically evaluate resident capabilities and care requirements. The findings from these assessments directly drive the development of the individualized care plan—a dynamic roadmap outlining specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, and time-bound (SMART) goals for the resident. For instance, if a resident is identified as a high fall risk, the care plan will detail specific interventions such as bed alarms, non-slip footwear, scheduled toileting assistance, and low-bed positioning. Documentation must be accurate, contemporaneous, and comprehensive, recording every clinical observation, medication administration, treatment provided, and resident response. In SNFs, thorough documentation is not only a legal safeguard proving adherence to the standard of care but also serves as the primary communication tool across shifts and disciplines. Regular evaluation and revision of the care plan ensure that as the resident's condition improves or declines, the nursing interventions adapt accordingly, maintaining legal compliance and high-quality clinical care.

headings.title: Rehabilitation and Restorative Nursing Care
headings.content: Rehabilitation and restorative nursing care are central to the mission of Skilled Nursing Facilities, focusing on helping residents maintain or regain maximum functional independence. While formal rehabilitative therapy is led by physical, occupational, and speech therapists, restorative nursing care is driven by the nursing staff 24 hours a day, 7 days a week. Restorative nursing encompasses specific nursing interventions designed to maintain the gains achieved during formal therapy and prevent functional decline. Examples include range-of-motion exercises, assistance with ambulation during routine hallway walks, retraining in self-care activities, proper positioning, and bowel/bladder training programs. Nurses collaborate closely with therapists to ensure that therapeutic techniques learned in the gym are reinforced during daily care routines on the residential unit. For example, if a physical therapist instructs a resident to use a specific walker and weight-bearing posture during transfers, the nursing assistant must reinforce this technique every time the resident gets out of bed. Furthermore, nurses monitor residents for fatigue, pain, or frustration during rehabilitation activities, providing emotional encouragement and modifying the pace of care when necessary. By embedding restorative principles into everyday nursing practice, SNFs prevent contractures, muscle atrophy, and pressure injuries, ultimately empowering residents to achieve a higher quality of life and greater autonomy.

headings.title: Regulations, Quality Standards, and Safety
headings.content: Operating a Skilled Nursing Facility requires strict adherence to local and international regulations, quality standards, and safety protocols to protect vulnerable residents from harm. SNFs are heavily regulated entities subject to regular inspections, licensing reviews, and accreditation standards to ensure compliance with health, safety, sanitation, and patient rights mandates. Safety in SNFs encompasses infection control, medication management, fall prevention, and emergency preparedness. Given the high density of elderly and immunocompromised individuals, robust infection control practices—such as rigorous hand hygiene, proper use of personal protective equipment (PPE), isolation protocols for infectious outbreaks, and environmental sanitation—are paramount to preventing healthcare-associated infections. Medication safety is another critical domain, requiring strict adherence to the 'rights' of medication administration, safe storage, and routine pharmacy reviews to minimize polypharmacy risks and adverse drug reactions. Fall prevention programs involve comprehensive risk assessments, environmental hazard reduction (e.g., adequate lighting, clutter-free hallways, secure grab bars), and individualized interventions. Additionally, emergency preparedness plans must be established and routinely drilled for scenarios such as fires, natural disasters, utility failures, or infectious disease pandemics. Nurses act as front-line enforcers of these quality standards, identifying safety hazards, reporting incidents or near-misses, and participating in quality improvement committees to continuously elevate the safety culture within the facility.

headings.title: Transition of Care and Discharge Planning
headings.content: Transition of care and discharge planning are vital processes that determine how successfully an SNF resident moves to their next phase of life, whether it is returning home, moving to assisted living, or transitioning to long-term custodial care. Effective discharge planning begins on the day of admission rather than waiting until the final days of the stay. The interdisciplinary team—led by nurses, social workers, and discharge coordinators—collaborates to evaluate the resident's ongoing needs, home environment, family support systems, and equipment requirements. If a resident is returning home, nurses ensure that the patient and their family caregivers receive comprehensive education regarding medication management, wound care, dietary modifications, and recognition of warning signs that necessitate medical follow-up. Home assessments or physical therapy evaluations of the home environment may be conducted to recommend necessary structural modifications, such as ramps, grab bars, or widened doorways. For residents transitioning to long-term care within the facility, discharge planning focuses on comfort, palliative care integration, and maintaining familiar daily routines. Coordination with outpatient services, primary care physicians, and community health nurses is essential to ensure a seamless handoff of clinical information, preventing gaps in care that could lead to avoidable hospital readmissions. Through thorough preparation, education, and inter-agency communication, the nursing team ensures that every resident experiences a safe, dignified, and well-supported transition.
